nodes.label: collectTagIndex
nodes.doc: collectTagIndex records which tag slugs will get a page, so a chip rendered during the walk knows whether its destination exists. Runs pre-walk, over docPages only - blog posts are not collected until the walk, so a blog-only tag simply keeps its search chip.

nodes.label: writeTagPage
nodes.doc: writeTagPage renders one synthesized page and records it everywhere the site tracks output. srcRel carries the "/_index.md" synthesized-page marker so renderPage knows there is no source to view or edit, and so rootPrefix climbs the right number of levels.

nodes.label: codeTeaser
nodes.doc: codeTeaser previews a tour example: skip the leading comment block and blank lines, then take the first several real lines - so the card shows code, not the header comment.

nodes.label: collectDemos
nodes.doc: collectDemos maps each concept docSlug to the FIRST tour step that demonstrates it (its title + card anchor), pre-walk, so renderFile can inject a "see the demo" callout on the matching concept page.

nodes.label: playgroundLink
nodes.doc: playgroundLink deep-links src into the playground editor via a #source= fragment, so the code stays client-side, never hitting server/CDN. The payload is a version byte plus url-safe unpadded base64; "0" is the uncompressed variant, which is what a producer with no DEFLATE implementation emits - this renderer and the page bundle (src/site/run-example.ts) both encode here, while the playground's own Share button emits the compressed "1". internal/playground/share.go decodes all of them.

nodes.label: renderPlayground
nodes.doc: renderPlayground writes gen/playground/index.html from the hand-authored playground.html, injecting the shared nav at its <!-- site-nav --> placeholder. The playground is standalone (custom head, wasm, own scripts), so it skips renderPage(); templating just the nav keeps it in lockstep with every other page. Its bottom chrome is the console status bar (in playground.html), not the docs footer.

nodes.label: tourDocSlug
nodes.doc: The doc cross-link is one line, `// doc: <slug>|<label>`, because a slug with no label renders a link with nothing to click.

nodes.label: tourMeta
nodes.doc: tourMeta reads one `// key: value` line from a step's header. The metadata lives in the step file so adding a step is one file, not two places that can disagree.

nodes.label: tourSrc
nodes.doc: tourSrc reads one curated example from tour/ (cwd-relative, build-time only; the files aren't written - their content rides into the page as teaser + deep-link).

nodes.label: tourSteps
nodes.doc: renderTourPage writes gen/tour/index.html: a numbered card grid walking a newcomer through magusfiles and Buzz. Synthesized (no .md source), so renderPage()'s srcRel guards drop the provenance/edit chrome. tourSteps is the ordered curriculum, shared by the tour page and collectDemos (which inverts each step's docSlug into a "see the demo" callout on the matching concept page).

nodes.label: demo
nodes.doc: The one target: it prints values the functions above compute. `run demo` evaluates them for real (the calls run inside the string interpolation), so the trace shows the actual numbers, not placeholders.

nodes.label: fact
nodes.doc: Recursion again, building a product. `eval fact(10)` -> 3628800.

nodes.label: fibo
nodes.doc: Recursion, the classic. `eval fibo(30)` computes 832040 in a real bytecode VM.

nodes.label: reduce
nodes.doc: Higher-order: a function that takes a function, invoked with an inline closure. `eval sum([2, 4, 6, 8])` -> 20.

nodes.label: ci
nodes.doc: The conventional anchor. Kept to lint here so the plan stays short.

nodes.label: go_lint
nodes.doc: A cheap check. It stays at the default of one slot; several like it run at once.

nodes.label: js_lint
nodes.doc: The greedy one: reserve 4 slots AND tell eslint to actually use 4 threads.

nodes.label: lint
nodes.doc: lint fans out to both. The scheduler runs the 1-slot check alongside other small work, but quiets the queue around js-lint's 4-slot reservation.

nodes.label: release
nodes.doc: A stand-in release, so `graph` shows the exclusive policy in context.

nodes.label: test
nodes.doc: Both of these need build. In the plan it appears once, not twice.

nodes.label: generate
nodes.doc: The umbrella: ctx.glob collects every current AND future *-generate target as handles, and ctx.needs depends on them. glob("name") with no wildcard is shorthand for "anything ending in -name", so glob("generate") would read the same as glob("*-generate") here. A pattern matching nothing yields no handles, so needs of it is just a no-op.

nodes.label: generate_fast
nodes.doc: "*-generate" gathers the family; "!snapshot-generate" removes one member. Order does not matter - the negation applies to the union of the includes - and the result is deduplicated and sorted, so dispatch order never varies between runs.

nodes.label: proto_generate
nodes.doc: One target per generator, all sharing the -generate suffix.

nodes.label: proto_lint
nodes.doc: When a set is not a clean suffix family, skip the pattern and pass the target functions to ctx.needs directly. proto-all gathers just the proto- family (its generate and its lint), and nothing else - the handles say exactly which. Either way needs only ever takes handles: a function, or the handles glob resolves a pattern to.

nodes.label: snapshot_generate
nodes.doc: Excluding one member of a family.  Sooner or later a target belongs to a family by name but not by behavior. Here snapshot-generate re-records fixtures: it is slow and needs a live service, so running it from the umbrella would make `run generate` fail on a laptop with nothing listening. A leading "!" subtracts it.

nodes.label: ci
nodes.doc: Charms ride down needs() edges, so a single charm on the anchor reaches the whole plan: `run ci:rw` hands rw to format too. Try `run ci`, then `run ci:rw`.

nodes.label: format
nodes.doc: Read the active charm set with has_charm, then branch. (Most real spell ops do this flip internally, so you usually get rw for free; here it is spelled out so the plan shows the difference.)

nodes.label: mgs_getName
nodes.doc: A spell announces its name...

nodes.label: mgs_listTargets
nodes.doc: ...and lists its ops: a map of op name to handler. Each handler takes the Target being built and returns a Command (runs to completion) or a Service.

nodes.label: serve
nodes.doc: serve returns a Service, so magus treats it as a long-running, shared op: command   - the process magus forks in the foreground and supervises readiness - a probe polled until it exits 0 (the Kubernetes exec-probe model), so dependents wait for "actually up", not a fixed sleep stop      - a graceful shutdown, replayed to reap orphans after a crash Reached as a dependency (some target's ctx.needs), it runs in the background, shared by config fingerprint; run directly, it runs in the foreground.

nodes.label: build
nodes.doc: Compile the version-stamped server binary and type-check the client.

nodes.label: ci
nodes.doc: The conventional anchor `magus affected ci` keys off. It declares no work of its own; it fans out to lint, build, and test, which share the format -> generate -> preflight spine and each run once. Try `run ci` to see the plan.

nodes.label: format
nodes.doc: Format every language. These ops CHECK by default; run `magus run format:rw` to APPLY the fixes: the rw charm flips gofmt -l to -w, prettier --check to --write, buf format to -w. The charm rides down from the run, so no branch is needed here. (Try `run format` then `run format:rw` in the console to compare.)

nodes.label: generate
nodes.doc: The umbrella `generate` target pulls in every `*-generate` target with ONE pattern instead of listing each by hand: ctx.glob("*-generate") resolves to every target ending in -generate, and ctx.needs depends on those handles, so adding a `sql-generate` later needs no edit here. (glob is the pattern resolver; needs itself only ever takes handles. A pattern with no `*` is suffix shorthand, so "generate" would read the same here.) That is the payoff of naming targets by a shared convention. Try `run generate`.

nodes.label: image_build
nodes.doc: Build the container image from the compiled binary. Default: a single-arch image loaded into the local daemon. Under the `cd` charm: a multi-arch image pushed to the registry. Kept as its own target so `magus run image-build` works standalone.

nodes.label: ldflags
nodes.doc: A plain Buzz helper that assembles the -ldflags stamping the version into the server binary (used by build below). Try `ldflags(VERSION)` in the console to see Buzz evaluate it; the interpreter is real, only the build tools are stubbed.

nodes.label: lint
nodes.doc: The umbrella `lint` fans out across the whole family with one pattern.

nodes.label: preflight
nodes.doc: Gate the pipeline on a healthy workspace before anything builds.

nodes.label: proto_generate
nodes.doc: Codegen is one `*-generate` target per generator. Each is ordinary cached codegen: magus keys it on its inputs and its gen/** outputs, so it reruns only when those inputs change. (Contrast with a drift-gate target that verifies committed output is current on every run; that one would set skip_cache because its point is the check, not a cacheable artifact.)

nodes.label: proto_lint
nodes.doc: Linting is a `*-lint` set too, one target per toolchain, so `lint` can glob them the same way `generate` globs its generators. js-lint is split out on its own because it carries the load: eslint is the heavy one, so this target holds LINT_SLOTS slots and runs eslint with a matching --concurrency (the cheap buf/go checks stay at the default of 1 slot). `magus run lint:rw` applies the auto-fixable findings where a tool supports it (e.g. golangci-lint --fix).

nodes.label: release
nodes.doc: Ship a release: a needs() edge onto image-build, so it shows up in `graph`/`ls` as part of the DAG. Charms ride down needs() edges from the run, so `magus run release:cd` flows the cd charm into image-build and it switches to a multi-arch push. (magus.run(["image-build:cd"]) would instead invoke it imperatively with the charm pinned in the call, but an imperative call is not a static edge, so it would not appear in the graph. Both are valid; needs keeps the DAG complete.)

nodes.label: test
nodes.doc: Run both suites.

nodes.label: ci
nodes.doc: The conventional anchor, wired with ctx.needs like always.

nodes.label: deploy
nodes.doc: Another target in the same project is always an edge, never a nested run. A run holds its projects' locks for its whole life, so `magus\run(["release"])` here would wait on a lock its own caller holds and magus refuses it (MGS3007). magus\run is for driving a DIFFERENT project - `magus\run(["build", "web"])` - which the caller does not hold.

nodes.label: release
nodes.doc: A bespoke phase. It depends on ci through the same ctx.needs edge the canonical targets use, then does its own extra work.

nodes.label: stamp
nodes.doc: A target assembling build config from the stdlib the way a real one would: derive an artifact slug and compare two versions, then print them. `run stamp` computes each value for real.

nodes.label: lint
nodes.doc: One op, one base command, two charms that reshape it. `after` splices values in just past an anchor argument; `append` adds to the end. Both resolve to an index now, at author time, so adding a charm later never shifts another's patch.

nodes.label: mgs_listTargets
nodes.doc: A spell lists its ops: a map of op name to handler.

nodes.label: login
nodes.doc: Verb two: ACT. The same list, so the set logged into is by construction the set pushed to. A CI step is now one line with no shell parsing anything, and it is the same line you run locally.  TWO protections, and neither makes the other redundant. The token goes to the command on STDIN, so it never enters an argv magus persists. And it was read through magus\secret.read, so magus knows the value is a credential and redacts it from captured output - which covers what this file does not control: the command it

nodes.label: publish_registries
nodes.doc: The single source of truth. A typed helper, not a target: it returns [Registry], which a target could not. Every verb below reads it, so they cannot disagree about which registries a run involves - add one entry and all of them follow.

nodes.label: readable
nodes.doc: Probing with try/catch, because a provider signals "not available" by THROWING - $VAR unset for the built-in, a locked vault for a 1Password spell. Presence is not something a caller can test for without asking.

nodes.label: registries
nodes.doc: Verb one: LOOK. Reports where a push would go and whether the credentials are present - without needing any of them, and without ever printing a value.

nodes.label: select
nodes.doc: Selection is BY NAME. Positional indexing looks tempting and is a trap here: the charm decides the list's length, so index 1 is a valid registry under `prod` and out of range under `dev`. An unknown host is an error naming the valid ones rather than a silent no-op.

nodes.label: gate
nodes.doc: The judgment a real language buys you. A scanner reports whether a problem matches; a gate has to decide whether you can do anything about it today. Fail on what is actionable, report the rest, and carry on. Fail on what nobody can fix and someone will mute the gate within a week.

nodes.label: stamp
nodes.doc: A failure that is EXPECTED in a known situation. Building outside a checkout is real - a release tarball, a container build context - so it is caught and named once, here, rather than every caller remembering a check the type system never asked for.

nodes.label: tools
nodes.doc: Branching on the CODE, not the wording. MGS3003 is "tool not on PATH"; anything else is a failure this target has no answer for, so it is re-thrown rather than swallowed. Catching everything and continuing is how a gate stops being a gate.

nodes.label: inject
nodes.doc: Editing rather than producing. This page is hand-written and only a region of it is generated, so it is NOT an output magus owns - declaring it with writesFiles would let `magus clean` delete somebody's prose. modifiesExistingFiles hashes it without claiming it.

nodes.label: report
nodes.doc: Narrow on purpose. readsFiles replaces the project baseline for this target, so editing something outside data/ does not re-run it. Name every input the target reads: a glob you forget is a file whose change magus cannot see, and a stale hit is the result.

nodes.label: stamp
nodes.doc: THE CONTRADICTION. This target claims the same output as `report`. Nothing stops both from running, so whichever finishes last wins and the other's drift gate fails against a file it did not write - a failure that points at the wrong target and wastes an afternoon.  `magus doctor` refuses it up front with MGS1020 and names both claimants. An output has one owner. If two targets both need to contribute, they write separate files and a third target combines them.

nodes.label: tidy
nodes.doc: THE SECOND CONTRADICTION, and unlike `stamp` no static check can see it: this target writes a file it declared as an INPUT. The key is hashed from data/** before the body runs, so by the time the run finishes the key describes a tree that no longer exists. Nothing can reproduce that entry - not CI, not a teammate, not this machine a second later - and it still reported success.  `magus run tidy` fails it with MGS4007 and names the file. The fix is the line above in `inject`: say `ctx.modifiesExistingFiles("

nodes.label: both
nodes.doc: Both a and b need prep. prep runs once.

nodes.label: prep
nodes.doc: ctx.needs DEDUPES within a run: a needed target executes ONCE per invocation, however many targets need it. This is why `ci` fanning out to lint, build and test does not run `format` three times - and why a shared setup step is safe to name from every target that depends on it, instead of being hoisted somewhere awkward to avoid repetition.  It is per-INVOCATION, not per-machine: it is the dispatcher deduping a dependency graph, not the cache replaying a previous run. Run `both` and count the prep line - on

nodes.label: report
nodes.doc: Declares a charm so `report:loud` is a legal invocation. The body does not even read the charm - the point is that the KEY differs regardless, because the charm is part of the run's identity whether or not this target's code branches on it.

nodes.label: db
nodes.doc: The baseline. Everything in this command that the fingerprint covers - image, tag, port, env - is part of what makes it THIS service rather than another one.

nodes.label: db_other_port
nodes.doc: DOES NOT ADOPT db. One port differs, so the fingerprint differs, so this is a second container. That is correct rather than unfortunate: a dependent connecting on 5433 needs something listening on 5433, and silently handing it the 5432 instance would fail later and further away. If you meant to share, match the config; if you meant two databases, this is how you get them.

nodes.label: db_same
nodes.doc: ADOPTS db. Same image and tag, same port, same env - only the flag ORDER differs, and order is normalized before hashing. One container serves both.

nodes.label: mgs_listTargets
nodes.doc: One map of op name to handler, same as any spell: a handler returning a Service is what makes the op long-running and shared, rather than a separate kind of declaration.

nodes.label: channel
nodes.doc: The channel this run publishes to, and the assertion that the version belongs there.  Note what the two charms have in common: each checks the OPPOSITE side of one semver field. That is why naming both needs no special case beyond the guard above - a version either carries a prerelease component or it does not, so one of the two assertions would fail on its own anyway.

nodes.label: exclusiveCharms
nodes.doc: Two charms that answer one question are a mistake worth REPORTING, not resolving. WS is this workspace's own code prefix - magus refuses the MGS prefix, which is its closed catalog, so a workspace diagnostic can never render as though magus documented it.

nodes.label: publish
nodes.doc: TWO axes, one charm each, and neither answers the other's question:  cd                 deliver? Absent, this builds and pushes nothing. stable / unstable  which channel? Only read when cd is set.  The default among delivering modes is the harmless one, for the same reason a bare run pushes nothing: the commit channel adds an immutable tag and moves nothing, while a release moves a tag every consumer follows.

nodes.label: version
nodes.doc: The version this build would carry. Real magusfiles read vcs\describe(); a literal keeps the tour runnable with no repository behind it. Change it to "1.4.0" and watch which channels accept it.

nodes.label: agent_demo
nodes.doc: The subprocess half. A child cannot be handed a Go HTTP client, so magus binds a loopback endpoint for the run and the child is pointed at it. There is no gateway to install and no service to start: the listener belongs to this run and closes when it ends.  Note who decides which variable carries it. magus does NOT set one for you - you name it, because a tool with no base-URL knob should fail somewhere you can see it rather than silently talking to the real endpoint unauthenticated.  The URL carries a rand

nodes.label: after
nodes.doc: after inserts vals immediately after the first argv element equal to anchor.

nodes.label: append
nodes.doc: append adds vals to the end of the argv.

nodes.label: before
nodes.doc: before inserts vals immediately before the first argv element equal to anchor.

nodes.label: drop
nodes.doc: drop removes the first argv element equal to anchor. Named drop, not remove, to match the host charm.drop (where "remove" collides with the map method) so the two modules expose one name.

nodes.label: prepend
nodes.doc: prepend inserts vals at the front of the argv, in order.

nodes.label: set
nodes.doc: set replaces the first argv element equal to anchor with val.

nodes.label: ci
nodes.doc: The anchor `magus affected ci` keys off; fans out lint/build/test after format.

nodes.label: generate
nodes.doc: Regenerates MAGUS.md. Use the rw charm to keep the result; without it the engine's drift gate compares what regeneration produced against what is committed. The gate is not written here: index_generate declares MAGUS.md as its output, which is the whole declaration magus needs to check it.

nodes.label: index_generate
nodes.doc: Renders MAGUS.md (target catalog plus graph) from this magusfile.

nodes.label: attachPoint
nodes.doc: attachPoint places connector k of n along a box edge at k/(n+1), snapped to the grid, so connectors sharing a side stay independently traceable.

nodes.label: connectorPath
nodes.doc: connectorPath emits an orthogonal route with rounded bends. Diagonals are not representable here by construction, which is how the "no diagonal connectors" rule is enforced rather than merely documented.  A horizontal route leaves and enters on the left/right sides and crosses on a vertical segment at x = bend; a vertical route is the transpose. When the two points already share an axis the route degenerates to a straight line and no bend is drawn.

nodes.label: cssVarPalette
nodes.doc: cssVarPalette drives the diagram from custom properties defined in site.css, which map onto Pico's own variables. Only valid for an SVG inlined into the page; an -loaded SVG resolves these against nothing and falls back to the hardcoded light values.

nodes.label: defaultStyle
nodes.doc: defaultStyle names the baseline the way lightPalette() names its own. A customization states only what differs, since every other field already carries the value here: Style{ strokeWidth = 2.0 }.

nodes.label: edgeGeometry
nodes.doc: edgeGeometry resolves an edge to [x1, y1, x2, y2, horizontal]. Buzz has no tuple, and a five-int list beats threading five result params through the painters.

nodes.label: edgeSegments
nodes.doc: edgeSegments returns an edge's route as axis-aligned segments, each [x1, y1, x2, y2]. It mirrors connectorPath's branching exactly; the two must agree, or the overlap check below is validating a route nobody draws.

nodes.label: escapeSvg
nodes.doc: escapeSvg makes s safe as SVG text or as a double-quoted attribute value. lib/text has an escapeAttr that does the same job, but importing it does not bind when this module is reached through the magusfile's graph rather than run directly, and a renderer with no cross-module dependency is worth more here than three deduplicated lines.

nodes.label: findNode
nodes.doc: findNode returns the node with id, or null when the edge names something that is not there. validate reports that; render treats it as unreachable.

nodes.label: inlineDiagrams
nodes.doc: inlineDiagrams swaps a diagram reference in rendered HTML for the SVG itself, keyed by diagram id. Inlining is what makes a diagram follow the site's manual theme toggle: an -loaded SVG is a separate document and can only ever see prefers-color-scheme. Two reference forms are recognized, because the two audiences need different markup. A docs page carries ``, which GitHub renders as nothing and goldmark passes through untouched. The README carries a real so GitHub shows the

nodes.label: lightPalette
nodes.doc: lightPalette and darkPalette mirror the site's Pico theme resolved to hex, for the standalone .svg pair. Keep these in step with the --magus-diagram-* block in site.css: a reader toggling the site theme sees the CSS vars, a reader on GitHub sees these.

nodes.label: nodeFill
nodes.doc: nodeFill and nodeStroke implement the role-to-treatment table. Roles the table does not name fall back to the default treatment rather than failing: validate is where an unknown role should be caught, not the painter.

nodes.label: overlapLen
nodes.doc: overlapLen measures the shared extent of two 1-D spans, each given in either order.

nodes.label: overlappingConnectors
nodes.doc: overlappingConnectors reports each pair of edges that share a stroke line. Runs on generated layouts too: automatic placement is exactly where this goes wrong unnoticed.

nodes.label: renderDecision
nodes.doc: renderDecision paints the diamond. The label sits on the center line rather than the stacked layout a box uses: a diamond's widest run is its middle, so a two-line stack would push text out past the sloping sides.

nodes.label: renderEdgeLabel
nodes.doc: renderEdgeLabel places the label off the crossing segment with a 6px gap, never on the stroke. Labels are painted before nodes, so one that strays onto a box is covered rather than left sitting on the border as a fragment.

nodes.label: renderLegend
nodes.doc: renderLegend draws the strip below the figure. The design system puts it outside the diagram area, so callers size the viewBox with 60px of room at the bottom.

nodes.label: renderMarkers
nodes.doc: renderMarkers defines one arrowhead per connector kind. All three are always emitted: an arrowhead referencing a marker that was not defined renders as a bare line, and which kinds a diagram uses is not worth tracking to save 200 bytes.

nodes.label: renderSvg
nodes.doc: renderSvg paints the diagram and throws a joined validation report when any rule is broken, so a malformed diagram fails the docs build instead of shipping crooked.  Paint order is load-bearing: zones, then connectors and their labels, then nodes, then the legend. Connectors go under nodes so a stroke cannot cross a box face, and nodes go over labels so a mask that strays onto a box is hidden rather than clipped mid-glyph.  Style is defaulted rather than overloaded: a caller that only wants the design syste

nodes.label: replacePicture
nodes.doc: replacePicture rewrites each <picture> element whose markup mentions needle. Scanning for the element bounds beats a regex here: the srcset and img inside carry attributes in no fixed order, and a <picture> that does not mention the needle has to survive untouched.

nodes.label: resolveSide
nodes.doc: resolveSide turns "auto" into a concrete side by comparing box centers: the wider gap wins, so two boxes side by side connect left-to-right rather than looping over the top.

nodes.label: segmentsOverlap
nodes.doc: segmentsOverlap reports whether two axis-aligned segments run along the SAME line and share more than a point. Crossing at right angles is fine and common; running on top of each other is what makes two connectors impossible to tell apart.

nodes.label: sharedAttachPoints
nodes.doc: sharedAttachPoints reports connectors that land on the same point of the same box. Two edges may share a side, but only by declaring different slots of the same total.

nodes.label: snap
nodes.doc: snap rounds onto the 4px grid. Applied to derived geometry only; an authored coordinate that misses the grid is a validation error rather than something to silently fix.

nodes.label: twoBox
nodes.doc: twoBox is the smallest sound diagram: two boxes on one row, one connector between them. Tests mutate a copy of it so each one states only the rule it is about.

nodes.label: validate
nodes.doc: validate returns one message per broken rule, empty when the diagram is sound. These are the design system's non-negotiables plus the structural ones a renderer cannot paper over: an edge naming a missing node, two nodes occupying the same space, two connectors landing on the same point of the same box.

nodes.label: test
nodes.doc: test runs the in-file test blocks. --embedded because the suite calls module-private helpers (connectorPath, attachPoint) directly rather than only the exported surface - the routing rules are what break, and they are not reachable from outside.

nodes.label: main
nodes.doc: A closure assigning to a captured local: capture is by reference, so every read and write goes through one shared cell.

nodes.label: fibo

nodes.label: currentVersion
nodes.doc: currentVersion returns a module's highest STABLE released version, or "" when it has never had one. Compared on the PARSED major/minor/patch, not the tag text, because string order puts v0.10.0 before v0.9.0.  Prereleases are skipped: per semver.org item 9 a prerelease has LOWER precedence than the version it anticipates, so v0.4.0-rc1 is emphatically not v0.4.0 released and must not become the base the next version is computed from - otherwise cutting rc1 would silently advance everyone's floor.  Build met

nodes.label: isCandidate
nodes.doc: isCandidate reports whether v is one of the three versions nextFor offers, comparing the RELEASE part only - so v0.4.0-rc1 and v0.4.0+ci both count as the minor candidate. A prerelease of a legal next version is itself legal; that is how you cut an rc without first inventing a version nobody agreed to.

nodes.label: modulePath
nodes.doc: rewriteRequire points go.mod's require for module at version, preserving the line's indentation. The `replace` directive names the same module and must NOT be touched: it is the local-development path, ignored by every downstream consumer, and rewriting it would break building inside this repo. modulePath returns the path go.mod declares, or "" when it declares none.  Needed for Go's major-version suffix rule, which applies to the path: from v2 on it must end in /vN, so a v2.0.0 tag beside a go.mod still na

nodes.label: needsMajorSuffix
nodes.doc: needsMajorSuffix reports whether releasing major from the module at path would publish a tag Go cannot resolve.  From v2 on, Go wants the path to end in /vN, and `go get` resolves the path. A v2.0.0 tag beside a go.mod naming the v1 path is uninstallable, and semver has no opinion, so the survey offers that candidate like any other. A non-Go module passes "" and never hits the rule.

nodes.label: nextFor
nodes.doc: nextFor returns the three legal next versions for a module currently at cur. An unreleased module is treated as sitting at 0.0.0, so its candidates fall out of the same rule as everyone else's (0.0.1 | 0.1.0 | 1.0.0) rather than being a special case someone has to remember.

nodes.label: releasableModules
nodes.doc: releasableModules enumerates every independently-versioned project: one whose resolved spells declare a manifest (spells.Spell.Manifests, the language's go.mod/package.json/Cargo.toml/pyproject.toml equivalent) that is actually present in its directory - types.ProjectEntry.Manifests, read by the caller via magus\projects() and passed in as projects, already did the "does the candidate file exist" filesystem check. Taking the inventory as a parameter rather than calling magus\projects() itself keeps this mod

nodes.label: access
nodes.doc: WHY THIS SPELL DOES NOT USE magus\secret.grant, unlike spells/github/actions.  A grant attaches a credential to a request as a header VALUE: prefix + value, on one declared host. That fits a bearer token exactly, and the Actions cache spell was converted to it. It does not fit SigV4, for two independent reasons:  1. AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY is never sent. It is an HMAC key input - see the kDate chain in sign() - so the thing on the wire is a derived signature, not the credential. There is no header for magus t

nodes.label: amzTimestamp
nodes.doc: amzTimestamp formats the current UTC time as a SigV4 x-amz-date (YYYYMMDDTHHMMSSZ), handing the calendar math to the host time module (Go's time.Format under the hood). os.time() returns epoch millis as a double — exactly what the time module speaks — so it flows straight through with no conversion.

nodes.label: cache_key
nodes.doc: cache_key derives the object key from the spec hash (already unique per project; hex, so URL-safe — no extra encoding needed in the canonical URI). NOTE: cache-key format differs from spells/github/actions/spell.buzz on purpose: S3 folds CACHE_VERSION into the key string ("magus-<hash>-<version>"), while GHA keeps the version in a separate `version` request field. Do NOT change the emitted string here — it would invalidate every existing S3 artifact. Track the inconsistency for follow-up only.

nodes.label: deleteObject
nodes.doc: deleteObject removes one object by key (S3 DeleteObject, path-style). DeleteObject is idempotent, returning 204 No Content whether or not the key existed.

nodes.label: enabled
nodes.doc: enabled gates the provider on having credentials and a bucket. The cache probes this once and skips fetch/push entirely when false — no remote calls.

nodes.label: get_artifact
nodes.doc: get_artifact downloads the object for io.hash into io.dest. true on a hit (200), false on a miss (404) or when not configured.

nodes.label: getenv
nodes.doc: getenv reads one environment variable, returning "" when unset. NOTE: byte-identical to the getenv in spells/github/actions/spell.buzz. The duplication is intentional/temporary: there is no shared magus/... buzz helper module for it yet (extracting one needs the embed+register plumbing magus/charm uses). Track for follow-up; keep the two copies in sync.

nodes.label: hostOf
nodes.doc: hostOf extracts the Host header value (authority) from a base URL. SigV4 signs the host header, and the server recomputes the signature against the Host it receives — which Go derives from the URL — so this must equal the URL authority.

nodes.label: listPage
nodes.doc: listPage fetches one page of the bucket listing (S3 ListObjects v1, path-style) for objects under the magus- prefix, starting after marker (""=from the start). Cache keys are hex + literal — all RFC-3986-unreserved — so neither prefix nor marker needs percent-encoding, and the canonical query string (keys sorted: marker before prefix) is byte-identical to the one on the URL.  RAISES on a non-200 rather than returning "". It used to return "", which listing() reads as end-of-listing - indistinguishable f

nodes.label: listing
nodes.doc: listing is a fiber generator over every magus- object in the bucket. Each resume yields the next {key, lastModified} object, transparently fetching the next S3 page when the current one drains — marker pagination stays hidden behind the coroutine. It returns null when the listing is exhausted; since a real artifact is never null, the consumer drains it with a resume-until-null loop. The bucket's LastModified is the S3-side mtime, so no per-object HEAD is needed.

nodes.label: mgs_getName
nodes.doc: Named for the product (Amazon S3), not the capability it provides here. Its siblings are named the same way - github-actions, gitlab-ci - and "s3-cache" broke that by describing the job instead of identifying the thing, which reads as a different kind of entity in a list of spells. See CONTRIBUTING.md#naming.

nodes.label: prune
nodes.doc: prune evicts cache objects per a retention policy, enumerating them through the listing fiber. Inputs arrive via cb: older_than_secs : int  — evict objects older than this many seconds (0 = off) keep_last       : int  — keep only the newest N objects (0 = off) dry_run         : bool — report intended deletions without performing them The two bounds are additive — an object is doomed if it trips either — and the doomed set is keyed by object key so the overlap never double-deletes. Returns true onc

nodes.label: put_artifact
nodes.doc: put_artifact uploads the file at io.src as the object for io.hash. true on a 200 store, false otherwise. The payload hash is the file's SHA-256 (S3 verifies it against x-amz-content-sha256).

nodes.label: sign
nodes.doc: sign builds the signed request headers for an S3 path-style request. path is the canonical URI ("/bucket/key"); query is the canonical query string (keys sorted, "" for none); payloadHash is the hex SHA-256 of the body (EMPTY_SHA256 for a bodyless GET/DELETE). Returns the header map to hand extra/http.

This is the protobuf analogue of an API-contract gate: compose it into `lint` so a breaking .proto change fails the same read-only stage as go-vet and golangci-lint. Docker's own message is a complete diagnosis to anyone who already knows docker and an exit code to everyone else, so the hints turn it into the command to run. Registries disagree about the wording - Docker Hub says "authentication required", GHCR and most OCI registries say "unauthorized" or "denied" - so each phrasing gets an entry rather than one guess.  This is what a workspace shou

nodes.label: hadolint

nodes.doc: `docker --version` ends in a build hash (`29.3.1, build c2be9cc`) that moves with a rebuild of the same release, so patch extraction sheds it. And it is CLIENT-only - it exits 0 with no daemon - so `docker info` is what answers whether it is usable.  hadolint gets no readiness probe: linting a Dockerfile talks to no daemon, and gating it here would make a lint wait on a service it never uses.

nodes.doc: annotate raises a message that surfaces on the pull request, not just the log. Actions has no dedicated code field, so a diagnostic code leads the title where it stays greppable in the annotations list.

nodes.doc: cache_key derives the cache key from the spec hash. The hash already folds in the project path (see cache/hash.go), so it is unique per project and needs no extra namespacing — and being hex, it is URL-safe. NOTE: cache-key format differs from spells/aws/s3-cache/spell.buzz on purpose: GHA keeps CACHE_VERSION in a separate `version` request field, while S3 folds it into the key string. Do NOT change the emitted string here — it would invalidate every existing GHA cache entry. Track the inconsistency for

nodes.label: enabled
nodes.doc: enabled gates the whole provider on running under GitHub Actions. The cache probes this once and skips fetch/push entirely when false, so wiring this spell in a magusfile is a no-op everywhere except GHA - no remote calls, no exports.

nodes.label: escapeData
nodes.doc: escapeData encodes the characters Actions treats as structural in a command's message. A raw newline would end the command early and spill the rest into the log as loose text, and a failure's cause is usually the part after line one. Percent goes first, or it would corrupt the escapes introduced after it.

nodes.label: escapeProp
nodes.doc: escapeProp additionally encodes the separators between properties, so a title containing a comma or colon cannot be read as the start of another property.

nodes.label: get_artifact
nodes.doc: get_artifact downloads the cache artifact for payload.hash into payload.dest. Returns true on a hit (dest written), false on a miss or when not running under Actions.

nodes.label: getenv
nodes.doc: getenv reads one environment variable, returning "" when unset (os.env returns null for an unset var; the callers below test against ""). NOTE: byte-identical to the getenv in spells/aws/s3-cache/spell.buzz. The duplication is intentional/temporary: there is no shared magus/... buzz helper module for it yet (extracting one needs the embed+register plumbing magus/charm uses). Track for follow-up; keep the two copies in sync.

nodes.label: group_end
nodes.doc: group_end closes the current fold. Actions tracks a single open group, so the id is unused; it is in the contract for providers keyed by section name.

nodes.label: group_start
nodes.doc: group_start opens a fold. Actions has no expanded section: ::group:: always starts collapsed. A caller asking for an expanded one wants output the reader must not have to click for, so the group is skipped and the content stays inline. Folding it anyway would be worse - a hidden failure is one nobody sees.

nodes.label: has_token
nodes.doc: has_token reports presence WITHOUT resolving, so enabled() and the cache-path guards stay cheap and cannot prompt.

nodes.label: in_actions
nodes.doc: in_actions is the one condition the whole provider gates on. A private predicate rather than a call to enabled() because enabled is a spell OP - it takes the op signature - so the internal guards below cannot reuse it directly.

nodes.label: maskInRunnerLog
nodes.doc: maskInRunnerLog asks the RUNNER to redact value from its own log. magus already redacts the output it captures; this covers the half magus cannot reach - a later step, or an action that never ran under magus at all. It is not pure belt and braces: the runner auto-masks anything interpolated from `secrets.*`, but NOT a step output injected into env:, and not a token minted mid-job like the OIDC one below.  std\print rather than anything magus captures, for the same reason group_start above uses it: a workflo

nodes.label: mgs_getName
nodes.doc: "GitHub Actions" is the product's canonical name; the bare leaf "actions" named nothing on its own, and a spell's registered name has to stand alone - it is what `magus describe spells` and every diagnostic show, with no directory around it to supply the vendor. See CONTRIBUTING.md#naming.

nodes.label: oidcToken
nodes.doc: oidcToken mints an OIDC token for audience from the runner's token endpoint. Actions publishes the endpoint and its request token into the environment only when the job declares `permissions: id-token: write`, so an unset variable means a missing permission far more often than a broken runner - and the message says that rather than naming the variable.  The audience identifies the relying party: "sts.amazonaws.com" for AWS, the workload-identity-pool provider URL for GCP, whatever the trust policy on the ot

nodes.label: put_artifact
nodes.doc: put_artifact uploads the artifact at payload.src for payload.hash. Returns true on success or when another runner already stored the same key, else false.

nodes.label: quote_prefixes
nodes.doc: quote_prefixes declares the line prefixes that introduce a workflow command. magus captures subprocess output and replays it, so a dependency printing "::error::" would otherwise have the runner execute it and forge annotations. Returned once per run; magus does the per-line matching itself.

nodes.label: resolve_secret
nodes.doc: resolve_secret is the secret-provider contract, detected by name and invoked by magus\secret.read(). It receives the reference as payload.ref and returns a Secret.  `> Secret`, not `> str`: Buzz checks function signatures, so a provider returning the wrong shape fails to load rather than failing at the first read.

nodes.label: rpc
nodes.doc: rpc POSTs a JSON Twirp request to the named CacheService method and returns the host http response map ({status, body}).

nodes.label: token
nodes.doc: token reads ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN through the SECRET PROVIDER, not getenv.  That one-word difference is the whole fix. A value read with getenv is not a value magus knows is a credential, so this token was absent from the redaction set entirely - any run log, captured output or cached entry quoting it kept it in the clear, in CI. Reading it through the provider registers it, and magus masks it everywhere it writes.  Under Actions no provider is selected, so the built-in environment provider resolves this to

nodes.label: tokenURL
nodes.doc: tokenURL puts the audience on the runner's token endpoint. The separator is chosen rather than assumed: the endpoint arrives carrying ?api-version=2.0, so a hard-coded "?" would build a second query string and earn a 400 that names nothing.

nodes.label: workflowEnv
nodes.doc: workflowEnv reads a secret the workflow injected. There is no other way in, so a miss is a workflow-file edit rather than anything this run could recover from - which is why the error is the snippet to paste rather than a status.

nodes.label: apiBase
nodes.doc: apiBase is the endpoint to call, without a trailing slash. Trailing slashes are stripped because every URL below joins with "/" - GITHUB_API_URL arrives with one on some runners and without on others, and "//repos" is a 404 nobody would think to look for.

nodes.label: apiHost
nodes.doc: apiHost is the git remote host that pairs with apiBase, so a remote is recognized on an appliance and not only on github.com.  Derived from the endpoint rather than configured separately: an installation has ONE host, and two settings that must agree is one setting plus a way to get it wrong. "api.github.com" loses its "api." because github.com's API lives on a subdomain while an appliance serves both from the same name.

nodes.label: decodeThreads
nodes.doc: decodeThreads turns one page of GitHub's review-comment JSON into thread records.  jsonDecode returns a boxed value: a map of accessors over the payload. An array must be read through .listValue(), or the foreach walks the accessors instead of the rows.

nodes.label: find_review
nodes.doc: find_review reports the pull request open for this branch, or an empty number when there is none. A branch with no pull request is the ORDINARY state - most branches, most of the time - so it is never an error and never a reason a diff fails to open.

nodes.label: has_token
nodes.doc: has_token reports presence WITHOUT resolving, so the guards below stay cheap and cannot prompt - the same split github/actions draws for the same reason. A reader opening a diff must never be asked for a credential by the act of looking.

nodes.label: publish_review
nodes.doc: publish_review sends a batch of drafts as ONE review.  A batch rather than a call per comment, which is the whole shape of self-review: you read, you accumulate remarks, and only then decide the set is worth sending. Publishing each as it is written would send the first thought before the fifth changed your mind about it.  Returns the review id and the drafts it accepted, so the caller can mark exactly those published. A partial result is a real answer here: GitHub rejects an inline comment whose line is no

nodes.label: reply_review
nodes.doc: reply_review answers one existing thread, so a conversation can be finished without leaving.

nodes.label: reviewBody
nodes.doc: reviewBody assembles the payload GitHub's "create a review" endpoint takes.  The verdict arrives ALREADY RESOLVED. magus decides whether an approval is allowed - a review may never approve a change its own credential opened, and "we could not tell who opened it" resolves the same way - and it decides that in Go, because this file is workspace-authored and a rule living here could be edited out by the person it constrains. So this maps three provider-neutral words onto GitHub's event vocabulary and does no j

nodes.label: review_threads
nodes.doc: review_threads lists the inline comment threads already on the review, so a reader never leaves for the browser to find out what a colleague said.  This is the one function that makes magus depend on a host being reachable. Every failure returns an EMPTY list rather than throwing: a diff that will not open because GitHub is slow is a worse tool than one that shows the change and says nothing about the conversation.  Paged, because the default page holds 30 and a truncation here reads as "nobody commented af

nodes.label: slug
nodes.doc: slug turns a git remote URL into "owner/name", empty when it is not a remote of this host. nodes.label: viewerLogin

GitHub hands over the pull request's author in the payload find_review already fetches, but the token's own owner takes a second round trip. magus caches that for the life of the daemon and sets want_viewer only while its cache is empty, so this costs one call ever rather than one per diff opened. nodes.label: annotate
nodes.doc: annotate does nothing: GitLab has no in-log annotation syntax. Declaring the op and returning true says "this provider does not do that" explicitly, rather than leaving magus to infer it from a missing export.

nodes.label: enabled
nodes.doc: enabled gates the whole provider on running under GitLab CI, which sets GITLAB_CI=true for every job. magus probes this once, so wiring the spell unconditionally costs nothing anywhere else.

nodes.label: getenv
nodes.doc: getenv reads one environment variable, returning "" when unset (os.env returns null for an unset var; callers test against "").

nodes.label: group_start
nodes.doc: group_start opens a section. Unlike Actions, GitLab can show one expanded, so a caller asking for that gets it rather than having the fold skipped.

nodes.label: mgs_getName
nodes.doc: The registered name is the product's canonical name, because it is what identifies this spell everywhere magus lists one - it stands alone, with no directory around it to give it context. (That is a separate question from the source layout: `go` lives in spells/golang/ and both are right, because "golang" is the idiomatic directory name and "go" is the language's real name.)  The bare leaf "ci" failed that test twice over: it names no product, and it collided head-on with magus's own central concept - the c

nodes.label: nowSeconds
nodes.doc: nowSeconds is the wall-clock second every section marker carries. os.time() is epoch millis.

nodes.label: quote_prefixes
nodes.doc: quote_prefixes declares the line prefix that introduces a section marker, so replayed subprocess output cannot close a section magus opened or forge one. magus reads this once and does the per-line matching itself.

nodes.label: sectionID
nodes.doc: sectionID reduces an id to what GitLab accepts for a section name: letters, digits, underscore, dot, and dash. magus keys sections by project path, which contains slashes, so this is not optional.  strings.kebabCase does the whole job in Go rather than a character loop here: a spell should reach for the host modules, not reimplement them. It is lossier than strictly required (it lowercases, and folds _ and . to dashes) but every output is legal, which is what matters - the id is a key GitLab matches start a

nodes.label: replaceArgs
nodes.doc: replaceArgs derives the go mod edit flags for the module described by currentJSON. Each GoMod is the exact `go mod edit -json` result for a workspace module, captured by the go spell in the caller's context. Only replacements whose old path names a workspace module are touched; third-party replacements are deliberately preserved.

nodes.label: replaceWorkspaceModules
nodes.doc: replaceWorkspaceModules points every workspace-local requirement in this project's go.mod at its relative path, standing in for the go.work this repo does not have. Without rw it verifies and raises MGS1016; with rw the edit lands. `project` names the magus project in that remediation, which the context cannot supply.  modifiesExistingFiles, not writesFiles: as an output go.mod would be snapshotted and replayable, so a cache hit could restore a pre-release go.mod over the version bump `release` had just wri

nodes.label: workspace_go_mods
nodes.doc: The go spell arrives as a parameter because a spell file cannot import another spell (`magus/spell/go` is bound only for magusfiles), which is also why this file's header says the caller supplies the two ops it needs.

nodes.label: goModEdit
nodes.doc: Edit is offline: it "reads only go.mod; it does not look up information about the modules involved" (go help mod edit), so the same tree always yields the same bytes. The write charm is therefore rw, not relock.

nodes.label: goModJSON
nodes.doc: Captures Go's structured module view for the spell's higher-level Buzz helper. This is deliberately a separate read-only op: `-json` and `-print` are distinct Go modes, while go-mod-edit remains the one command that applies derived edits.

nodes.label: goModTidy
nodes.doc: Tidy resolves against the module proxy, and an import go.mod does not require yet arrives at latest, so its result turns on what upstream serves today rather than on this tree alone. The write charm is therefore relock, not rw.

nodes.label: goVulncheck
nodes.doc: Invoked directly rather than through `go tool`, for the same reason as golangCILint above: `go tool govulncheck` requires the binary in the module's tool block, and a workspace that had not put it there got "no such tool" - so the op could not run at all. On PATH it is pinned by whatever the workspace uses, and mgs_getVersionProbes records which.

nodes.label: golangCILint
nodes.doc: Invoked directly rather than through `go tool`: golangci-lint generates no code, so it has none of the generator/runtime lockstep that keeps protoc-gen-go pinned in go.mod. `go tool golangci-lint` also required the binary in the module's tool block, and a workspace that had not put it there got "no such tool" - the op could not run at all. On PATH it is pinned by whatever the workspace uses (mise, asdf, a system package), and the spell's version probe records which.

nodes.label: mgs_getTools

Asking for `patch` extracts the version and sheds all of that, so two machines running the same tool agree on a key. It narrows nothing anyone reasons about. Without it a .txtar was unclaimed - editing one invalidated no cache key and pulled no project into the affected set, so a CI run keyed on `magus affected` could not see a behavior test change at all, and a stale pass would replay from cache. nodes.label: has
nodes.doc: has reports whether haystack contains needle.  Buzz's str.indexOf returns NULL when the substring is absent, not -1, so comparing the result to a number raises "cannot compare null and int" rather than answering false. That is why this is a named helper instead of an inline comparison at four call sites.

nodes.label: mgs_getName

nodes.label: resolve_secret
nodes.doc: resolve_secret is the secret-provider contract, detected by name and invoked by magus\secret.read(). It receives the reference as payload.ref and returns a Secret.  `> Secret`, not `> str`: Buzz checks function signatures, so this one is enforced at compile time - a provider returning the wrong shape fails to load rather than failing at the first read. nodes.label: biomeCheck
nodes.doc: biome-check is biome's lint/analyze pass (eslint's role, if your project chose Biome over eslint+prettier - the magusfile decides which composes into lint, not this spell). --write and --reporter=github verified against the current Biome CLI docs (biomejs.dev/reference/cli).

nodes.label: biomeFormat
nodes.doc: biome-format is biome's formatter (prettier's role). Unlike prettier/ruffFormat, `biome format` has no --check flag to drop: it is read-only by default (reports differences, writes nothing) and --write applies them, so rw ADDS a flag instead of removing one.

nodes.label: devServer
nodes.doc: dev-server runs the project's package.json "dev" script via the package manager - framework-neutral (Vite, Next, webpack-dev-server, ...). No readiness probe is declared: the port and startup signal vary by framework, so guessing one would be wrong more often than right (readiness is optional - see services.md). A magusfile that needs to block on readiness for its specific dev server can declare its own service op instead.

nodes.label: eslint

nodes.label: mgs_listTargets
nodes.doc: mgs_listTargets is typed `any` (not {str: fun(Target) Command}) because dev-server mixes in a Service-returning op alongside the Command-returning ones.

nodes.label: preflight
nodes.doc: preflight is a no-op marker op (no command).

nodes.doc: tsc-build uses TypeScript's project-references incremental build mode (works even without declared references, via its own .tsbuildinfo cache), emitting per tsconfig outDir - see mgs_listProvidedGlobs.

nodes.label: tscClean
nodes.doc: tsc-clean mirrors tsc-build's project-references mode: --clean removes the declared outputs and the incremental .tsbuildinfo cache.

nodes.label: keepsSource
nodes.doc: keepsSource decides whether one lcov SF: path counts toward the figure.  Anchored at a path boundary, both forms: node:test writes paths relative to the cwd ("src/foo.ts") while other producers write absolute ones ("/w/src/foo.ts"). A bare substring test would also match "vendor/notsrc/...".  node_modules is excluded FIRST and separately, because the boundary anchor alone does not exclude it: a dependency that ships its own src/ directory gives "/node_modules/x/src/y.js", which contains "/src/" and so passe

nodes.label: mergePercent
nodes.doc: / mergePercent is percent over SEVERAL lcov reports of the same sources, / merged at line level so overlapping reports are not double counted.  It exists because a project whose tests run in more than one process gets one report per process, and those reports OVERLAP: every process that imports a shared module reports that module's whole line table, so summing their LF/LH counts that file once per process. The figure comes out looking like a weighted average of how many processes happened to touch each file

nodes.label: percent
nodes.doc: / percent is the covered-line percentage across an lcov report, as a string / rounded to one decimal ("87.6"). / / keep filters by source path so the figure describes code someone wrote: / a report routinely carries dependencies and generated files, and counting / those measures the ecosystem rather than the project. / / Raises rather than reporting 0.0 when nothing matched, because a zero and a / mismatched filter look identical to a badge and only one of them is a fact.

nodes.label: audit
nodes.doc: audit scans the current project and fails ONLY on findings that are actionable today. Everything else is printed and carried. Throws to fail the calling target.

nodes.label: hasInstallablePatch
nodes.doc: hasInstallablePatch reports whether any published version of pkg satisfies the advisory's patched range AND is old enough to clear the cooling period - that is, whether a fix could land today.  `pnpm view <pkg> time --json` returns a version -> ISO-8601 map plus the non-version keys "created" and "modified", which are skipped. A version that fails to parse is skipped rather than fatal: an odd tag upstream must not take a build down.

nodes.label: isBlockingSeverity
nodes.doc: isBlockingSeverity reports whether a severity is worth failing over at all. moderate and low are reported and never fatal: the noise floor of a dependency tree lives there, and a gate that cries about it teaches people to stop reading it.

nodes.label: changedSince
nodes.doc: changedSince returns the files whose bytes moved since `before` was taken: created, modified, or deleted. A file that was already dirty and stayed byte-identical is NOT drift - it is uncommitted work the generators did not touch, which is the whole point.

nodes.label: expand
nodes.doc: expand flattens a mixed list of file and directory paths into the files under them, so a gate can name a generated TREE the way its outputs are declared and not have to know which entries are directories. A path that does not exist yet is dropped; changedSince notices it when the generator creates it.

nodes.label: hashes
nodes.doc: hashes digests every file under paths, taking the "before" side of a gate.

nodes.label: buildDoc
nodes.doc: buildDoc is the pure transform: files in, one document out. It reads no clock and sends no request, so two runs over the same inputs produce identical bytes.

nodes.label: encode
nodes.doc: encode renders the document. jsonEncode sorts keys, which is what makes the bytes stable across runs and across machines.

nodes.label: fetchAll
nodes.doc: fetchAll downloads the product list and every product into dir, one file each.  Kept apart from the transform so a network failure stops here rather than being folded into a build that would then publish a half-refreshed snapshot.

nodes.label: loadReleases
nodes.doc: loadReleases projects releases/*.yaml into the registry, newest first. The same list public/release/index.json serves, carried here so a new binary needs one file rather than two half-synced ones.

nodes.label: productSlugs
nodes.doc: productSlugs lists the cached responses, sorted, so the output does not depend on what order the filesystem hands them back.

nodes.label: safeSlug
nodes.doc: safeSlug reports whether a product name from the upstream API may be used as a filename.  The name is attacker-controlled in the only sense that matters here: it arrives in a third-party HTTP response, and this runs in a CI job holding MAGUS_REGISTRY_KEY. fs\join NORMALIZES a path, it does not confine one, so a name of `../../x` resolves cleanly to a write outside the cache directory. The check is a whitelist rather than a blacklist of separators because that is the form that stays correct when a platform a

Not built because no source for it clears the bar the version list clears. nodes.label: extract
nodes.doc: extract pulls a version out of a probe line.  magus already ships exactly this - spells.ExtractVersion, regex-based, and it already handles go's glued `go1.26.5` and golangci-lint's build-identity padding - but no Buzz binding exposes it, so the two cases needed here are hand-rolled. Delete this the day `semver\extract` lands; it is a binding over tested code, not a new concept.

nodes.label: observe
nodes.doc: observe prints one line about one tool. It never throws.  Within-line first, because "3 patches behind on 1.26" is a fact about a release you already chose, while "1.27 exists" is a fact about a decision nobody here is qualified to make for you. Other lines are named, never counted: a count reads as a backlog, and moving lines is one decision however many releases upstream cut on the far side.

nodes.label: probe
nodes.doc: probe runs a binary's version command and returns the extracted version, or "" when the tool is absent or says nothing version-shaped. Absent is not a finding: a tool this repo does not install is not out of date.

nodes.label: report
nodes.doc: report observes every wired toolchain. It prints and never throws: nothing here is a defect in the tree, it is information about the world outside it, and deciding what to do about that belongs to whoever reads it.

nodes.label: tagsOf
nodes.doc: tagsOf lists the release tags a remote carries, as bare versions.  ONE fork per remote, and the caller holds the result. A remote is a distinct network endpoint so two of them cannot share an invocation, but nothing should ever ask the same remote twice in a run - the parsed list answers every question about that tool.  GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 because ls-remote inherits the caller's git config and credential helpers. That is a supply-chain plus (no new trust, no new secret) and a hang risk: a helper that deci

Symlinks and devices are skipped, matching uncompress. opts keys: threads (int, parallel decode workers; 0 or omitted = auto).

nodes.label: archive.read_file

nodes.label: crypto.base64_decode_bytes

nodes.label: crypto.hmac_sha256
